sources.title: James Forsyth, A History of the Peoples of Siberia, Cambridge University Press excerpt
sources.note: Scholarly overview of Siberia before Russian expansion, environmental variety, many Indigenous languages and the danger of treating the region as one people.

sources.title: Edward Vajda, Typological Accommodation in Central Siberia, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Language families, multilingual contact, and distinct Ugric, Samoyedic, Yeniseian, Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic communities.

sources.title: W. K. Matthews, Palaeoasiatic Languages, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Distinct Chukotko-Kamchatkan, Yukaghir, Nivkh and Ket languages; used only as a linguistic classification, not a medieval population census.

sources.title: Thomas T. Allsen, The Mongols and Siberia, Cambridge History of the Mongol Empire
sources.note: Mongol political, administrative and economic relations with forest peoples, northern products in Eurasian trade and resulting transformations.

sources.title: Allen J. Frank, The western steppe: Volga-Ural region, Siberia and the Crimea, Cambridge History of Inner Asia
sources.note: Golden Horde fragmentation, regional yurts and formation of fifteenth-century successor states including the Siberian Khanate.

sources.title: Arthur Hatto, The World of the Khanty Epic Hero-Princes, Cambridge University Press excerpt
sources.note: Medieval Russian descriptions of multiple Yugra principalities, princes, retinues, social ranks and fortified river settlements; later-recorded epic evidence is separately labeled.

sources.title: Janet Martin, Treasure of the Land of Darkness, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Medieval Eurasian demand for luxury fur and the special importance of northeastern Europe and northwestern Siberia.

sources.title: Michal Biran, Forced Migrations and Slavery in the Mongol Empire, Cambridge World History of Slavery
sources.note: War captives, forced movement, multiple dependency statuses, slave markets and possibilities of manumission under Mongol rule.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Arctic Lands and Peoples
sources.note: Distinct Arctic peoples, tundra, forest and coastal ecologies, and long-term hunting and fishing adaptations.

sources.title: William Fitzhugh and Aron Crowell, Crossroads of Continents: Cultures of Siberia and Alaska, Smithsonian Institution Press
sources.note: Museum synthesis of northeastern Siberian dwellings, clothing, tools, domestic life and oral traditions; used as later comparative evidence, never silently projected backward.

sources.title: Smithsonian Arctic Studies Center, Culture Contact and Transformations
sources.note: Long-term exchange and transformation in Arctic material technology; museum evidence used with chronology warnings.

sources.title: Natalia Fedorova and colleagues, Reindeer Imagery in the Making at Ust-Polui in Arctic Siberia, Cambridge Archaeological Journal
sources.note: Archaeological argument for transport reindeer and later large-scale pastoralism in northwestern Siberia, with regional and chronological limits.

sources.title: Slepchenko and colleagues, Opisthorchiasis in infant remains from medieval Zeleniy Yar, Memorias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz
sources.note: Twelfth- to thirteenth-century lower Ob infant burial, fur, hide, birchbark and parasite evidence for minimally cooked fish; direct but just before the atlas interval.

sources.title: Alexander Gusev, Rich Burials of Children at Zeleny Yar, Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia
sources.note: Medieval lower Ob child burials with differentiated goods and cautious discussion of high status.

sources.title: Seo and colleagues, Archaeoparasitological Analysis of Nadym Gorodok, Journal of Parasitology Research
sources.note: Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century cultural-layer parasite evidence bearing on diet, movement and health, not proof of a latrine or sewer.

sources.title: Shiyatov and colleagues, Construction history and timber use of Nadymskiy Gorodok, Journal of Archaeological Science
sources.note: Dendrochronology and construction evidence for a long-lived wooden subarctic settlement; building phases do not define one ethnicity.

sources.title: Gusev, Plekhanov and Podosenova, A Medieval Burial at Lake Parisento, Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia
sources.note: Child burial on the Gydan Peninsula with imported metal goods and an explicit statement that Arctic western Siberian archaeology remains sparse.

sources.title: Bagashev and colleagues, A Medieval Yakut Burial Near Lake Atlasovskoye, Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia
sources.note: Radiocarbon-dated fourteenth- to fifteenth-century Kulun-Atakh burial, birchbark, trauma, heavy physical stress and alternative warrior or enslaved-status interpretations.

sources.title: Crubezy and colleagues, Early Yakut Burials of the 14th-17th Centuries, Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia
sources.note: Early Sakha burials and livestock-herding evidence in pre-Cossack Yakutia, used as a localized Lena case study.

sources.title: Keyser and colleagues, The genetic legacy of legendary and historical Siberian chieftains, European Journal of Human Genetics
sources.note: Fifteenth- to nineteenth-century Yakut burial dataset and explicit warning that rare frozen-ground burials are socially and chronologically unrepresentative.

sources.title: Simon Franklin, The changing environment, Writing, Society and Culture in Early Rus, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Absence of plausible indigenous scripts in adjacent northern forest regions and distinction between script-bearing imported objects and local literacy.

sources.title: Arthur Hatto, The World of the Khanty Epic Hero-Princes, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Eighteen Khanty heroic epics collected much later and studied as oral tradition; useful for continuity but not verbatim medieval transcription.

sources.title: Robert G. Bednarik and colleagues, Angara Style Rock Art, Cambridge Archaeological Journal
sources.note: Ket and Evenki oral histories, collective memory and material culture, with scholarly cautions about linking later traditions to archaeological populations.

sources.title: Sikora and colleagues, An ancient DNA perspective on Russian conquest of Yakutia, Nature
sources.note: Archaeological and biological evidence for Sakha communities before and after Russian conquest beginning in the seventeenth century, including major disruptions and continuity.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography SB RAS, Museum of History and Culture of Peoples of Siberia and the Russian Far East
sources.note: Official museum framing of many distinct Siberian and Far Eastern archaeological and ethnographic traditions, including medieval states, local religions and material technologies.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas umbrella for diverse Indigenous Siberian peoples, 1279 to 1530; never one nation.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id siberians is preserved only as a display key for a circa 1279 to 1530 culture feature.
The imported summary about ethnic Russians or Siberiaks is rejected as anachronistic for the medieval feature.
The feature is an umbrella or residual basemap bucket, not one state, nation, people, language or stable cultural horizon.
Khanty, Mansi, Samoyedic, Yeniseian, Tungusic, Turkic, Mongolic, Yukaghir, Nivkh and Chukotko-Kamchatkan contexts remain distinct.
The 1279 to 1300 and 1300 to 1400 geometries are identical; later contractions reflect changing imported partitions, not migrations measured by the polygon.
Golden Horde, Yuan, White Horde, Sibir, Oirat, Chagatai, Moscow and Ming polygons are neighboring atlas records and are not aliases for the target.
The 1530 seam fragments into named peoples, overbroad states and blank space. It is not a conquest, extinction or valid successor chain.
No in-period written sample is supplied because no single Siberian language existed and no securely attributable 1279 to 1530 component text was found; adjacent court scripts are not substituted.
